newsitem.title: CAMBODIA: FEATURE - Cambodia peace marred by landmine legacy.
newsitem.headline: FEATURE - Cambodia peace marred by landmine legacy.

text.p: An end to fighting was just months away in this bitterly contested Khmer Rouge stronghold when Khut Cheng, a thin, weary 50-year-old widow, got her final taste of Cambodia's long-running civil war.
In March, her 10-year-old son, Soeun, was running behind her house with playmates when he stepped on a small anti-personnel landmine.
He lost a leg and now moves about on worn wooden crutches.
"How I pity my son," Khut Cheng told Reuters, as Soeun sat quietly nearby.

"He lost his leg at such a young age. That is why I want UNTAC to come back and destroy these mines," she said, referring to the United Nations Transitional Authority in Cambodia, which oversaw 1993 national elections.

Khut Cheng, who lost her husband to illness a decade ago, was happy when thousands of breakaway Khmer Rouge troops that control her hometown of Phnom Malai, 300 km (187 miles) northwest of Phnom Penh, joined the government in November.
The defections have given the country its best chance of lasting peace following decades of war, including the brutal 1975-1979 "killing fields" regime of the Khmer Rouge.
But for Khut Cheng and millions of other Cambodians, the conflict will not end until all landmines are destroyed.
An estimated six to 10 million landmines exist in Cambodia, almost one for each of the country's 10.5 million people.
The International Committee of the Red Cross (ICRC) says Cambodia has the highest incidence of mine amputees per capita in the world -- roughly one per 325 people.
Mine clearance crews have been painstakingly removing landmines throughout much of the country, but up to now, Khmer Rouge-controlled areas have been off-limits.
With the recent defection of Khmer Rouge fighters, there is new, uncharted territory in government hands that needs mine clearance, aid workers say.
Breakaway leader Ieng Sary, former foreign minister during the Khmer Rouge regime, has asked for help in the task.
"There are a lot of mines around both Phnom Malai and Pailin, especially on Route 10 and I am ready to welcome both government and international agencies to clear mines," he said recently.

Khroch Rorn, a senior Khmer Rouge guerrilla who joined the defectors, said mines were the biggest enemy in the conflict against the government, which has simmered since the Maoist group reneged on a 1991 peace pact and fought the coalition government elected in 1993.
"Most solders here are injured by mines. We were rarely wounded by bullets or bombs. Mines are a very complicated problem, created by both us and the government."
Privately, aid agencies say they are under pressure to channel funding into areas like Phnom Malai, but that they have made no formal decisions yet.
The government says it may be willing to clear the area of mines, but that it is waiting for studies on the problem, formal requests for mine clearance activities and aid funds.

Phan Sothy, chief of staff of the Cambodian Mine Action Centre (CMAC), the national coordinating body for mine clearance activities, said no official decision has been made on clearing mines in former Khmer Rouge areas.

He said the scope of the landmine problem in former Khmer Rouge territory was not entirely clear, but that a planned survey and a team of newly acquired, mine-sniffing dogs should help future work in the area.
"We don't know how many hectares of mine fields there are, or what kind of mines there. But the Khmer Rouge know better than we do, so we will cooperate with them to clear the mines."
Him Vandy, a spokesman for CMAC, said it was impossible to know the extent of mined areas that were formerly under Khmer Rouge control.
However, aid workers say some Khmer Rouge guerrillas have kept clear maps of where mines are laid.
But the process is expected to be slow.
In its 1996 mid-year report, CMAC said it had cleared 27 square km (10 sq miles) of mine fields in government areas, but that 1,880 sq km (705 sq miles) remained.
"Mine clearance has been slow, arduous, dangerous and chronically under-financed," a recent ICRC report noted.
To Tao Ku, a 40-year-old farmer, that is bad news.

"I used to be a soldier from 1972 to 1982 and I lost my right leg when I stepped on mine in 1982. Now I am a farmer living with my wife and six children and my life is too difficult for me to feed them," he said.
